 Western Pacific countries show strong interest in working together on access to essential medicines
WHO / J.Kelly Halina 
Mr Lluis Vinyals Torres moderates the ministerial roundtable on essential medicines at the seventy-seventh session of the WHO Regional Committee for the Western Pacific. 
 © 
 Credits 
 Western Pacific countries show strong interest in working together on access to essential medicines
 Health ministers at the Regional Committee support voluntary collaboration to improve access to safe, effective, quality-assured and affordable health products
 21 October 2026 
 News release 
 Manila 
 Reading time: 
 Health ministers 
and senior delegates from across the Western Pacific Region, home to nearly 2.2 
billion people, have expressed strong support for exploring voluntary regional 
collaboration to improve access to safe, effective, quality-assured and affordable 
health products. This was the key outcome of a ministerial roundtable at the 
seventy-seventh session of the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional 
Committee for the Western Pacific, the regional governing body. 
 Convened at the 
request of the Philippines and facilitated by the Division of Health Systems 
and Services at the WHO Regional Office for the Western Pacific, the roundtable 
explored how countries could work together to respond to mounting challenges 
affecting access to medicines and other critical health supplies. 
 Latest WHO 
estimates show that nearly 600 million people in the Region, or 27% of the 
population, faced financial hardship from health spending, with cost of 
medicines a major driver of out-of-pocket spending. Geopolitical and economic 
crises are adding pressure on supply chains and health budgets, making access 
to medicines harder to sustain. 
 "Access to 
safe, effective, quality-assured and affordable medicines is fundamental to 
universal health coverage," said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO 
Director-General, while addressing the gathering. "Strong national 
pharmaceutical systems must remain the foundation. But some problems cannot be 
solved by countries acting alone. WHO stands ready to support Member States in 
analyzing the options, learning from other regions, and developing solutions 
that reinforce national systems and reflect the realities of the Western 
Pacific Region." 
 The 
Director-General pointed to Africa's regulatory harmonization efforts and the 
African Medicines Agency as examples of what countries can achieve together. 
The Pan American Health Organization, the WHO Regional Office for the Americas, 
shared lessons from over 40 years of rich experience with its Regional Revolving Funds . The WHO Regional Office 
for Europe, which also covers Central Asia, described how collaboration among 
countries and stakeholders can improve access to medicines, highlighting 
regional initiatives and lessons from its Novel Medicines Platform . 
 WHO outlined five 
areas where regional collaboration could complement national efforts: 
 1) stockpiling 
rare and critical products such as antidotes and antitoxins; 
 2) cooperation 
through regulatory reliance and recognition; 
 3) sharing 
intelligence to better deal with shortages and supply security; 
 4) aggregating 
demand and building collaborative procurement; and 
 5) collective 
action to help emergency preparedness. 
 Member States 
agreed that any collaboration should be country-led, voluntary, and 
complementary to national systems and existing mechanisms. They stressed the 
role of strong national regulatory systems in ensuring the quality, safety and 
efficacy of health products. 
 Several countries 
called for better demand forecasting and market transparency. Japan, for 
example, asked for clarity on the scope of proposed regional collaborations, 
and for the roles of partners such as Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, and the 
Coalition of Epidemic Preparedness Innovations to be considered. Many saw 
subregional groupings, including and particularly the Association of Southeast 
Asian Nations (ASEAN), as a practical basis for taking collaboration forward. 
 ASEAN member 
countries also pointed to existing initiatives on drug, vaccine and diagnostic 
security and self-reliance, including ASEAN Drug Security and Self-Reliance, 
ASEAN Vaccine Security and Self-Reliance and ASEAN Diagnostics Security and 
Self-Reliance, which could offer lessons for improving market transparency and 
procurement. 
 Five regulatory 
authorities in the Region (Australia, Indonesia, Japan, the Republic of Korea 
and Singapore) are WHO Listed Authorities, recognized for meeting international 
standards. Singapore and Indonesia highlighted that regulatory cooperation 
could reduce duplication of regulatory work, facilitate more timely access to 
new and life-saving medicines, and make markets more attractive to 
manufacturers. Australia, which works across both the ASEAN and Pacific 
subregions, offered to share lessons from regulatory partnerships. 
 Malaysia proposed 
a pooled procurement pilot, starting with a few essential medicines for which 
countries share clear needs. The Marshall Islands and Papua New Guinea welcomed 
the idea and offered to be pilot sites, saying it was time to move from discussion 
to action. Palau, Samoa, Tonga and Tuvalu also voiced support, with Samoa 
speaking for many in calling for an equitable voice for Pacific island countries and areas. 
 "I am so 
encouraged by the collegiality and candour displayed by our Member States on 
this timely topic," said Dr Saia Ma’u Piukala, WHO Regional Director for 
the Western Pacific. "Countries have issued a strong call to action, 
requesting WHO to chart a concrete plan with clear milestones. It’s clear that 
we need to demonstrate measurable progress that benefits the Region, especially 
for countries that currently face significant constraints in accessing the 
medicines and other commodities they need.”  
 "While the 
roundtable was exploratory, it showed 
growing interest in practical and voluntary approaches to shared 
challenges," said Lluis Vinyals Torres, Director of the Division of Health 
Systems and Services at the WHO Regional Office for the Western Pacific. 
"WHO will continue working with Member States through further technical 
analysis and consultation, taking into account country needs and existing 
mechanisms, to move from ad hoc responses to planned arrangements. Working 
together reflects the multilateral approach to health that WHO in the Western 
Pacific promotes for over a quarter of the world population." 
 For more 
information and/or to arrange media interviews, contact wprocom@who.int

Division of Health Systems and Services at the WHO Regional Office for the 
Western Pacific can be accessed at Division of Health Systems
